n: At Gilgal, Samuel gives a farewell address. He reminds the people he has done what they asked and given them a king.
Samuel notes the change in leadership: the king now leads them, while Samuel has grown old after serving them faithfully since childhood.

f.w: from my childhood unto this day

n: Samuel invites anyone to accuse him of stealing, cheating, oppressing, or accepting bribes. A leader's integrity should be open to inspection. Compare King Benjamin's similar words.
The people confirm that Samuel has never cheated, oppressed, or taken anything from anyone.
Samuel calls the Lord and the king as witnesses to his innocence, and the people agree. Their own testimony will make their demand for a king harder to justify.
Samuel turns to history: it was the Lord who raised up Moses and Aaron and brought Israel out of Egypt.
Like a lawyer in court, Samuel asks the people to stand still while he presents evidence of the Lord's righteous acts.
When Jacob's descendants suffered in Egypt and cried to the Lord, He sent Moses and Aaron to bring them to this land.

f.w: When Jacob was come into Egypt

n: But when they forgot the Lord, He let enemies like Sisera, the Philistines, and Moab oppress them. This is the repeating cycle of the book of Judges.
Then they would confess their idolatry and plead for deliverance, promising to serve the Lord.
The Lord sent deliverers — Jerubbaal (Gideon), Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel himself — and gave them safety. God had always provided leaders without a king.

f.g: Unknown otherwise; the Greek Septuagint reads “Barak.”

n: Yet when Nahash threatened, they demanded a king — even though the Lord their God was already their King.

f.w: when the LORD your God was your king

n: Here is the king you chose and wanted, Samuel says — and the Lord has allowed it.
If both people and king fear the Lord, serve Him, and obey, all will go well. The monarchy can still succeed under God.

f.g: to revere and respect God deeply

n: But if they rebel, the Lord's hand will be against them as it was against their ancestors. Having a king does not exempt them from covenant consequences.

f.w: the hand of the LORD be against you

n: Samuel tells them to watch a great sign the Lord is about to perform.
Wheat harvest falls in the dry season, when rain is very rare in Israel. A sudden thunderstorm would be an unmistakable sign — and could ruin the harvest.

f.g: Around May–June, when rain almost never falls in Israel.

n: Samuel prays, and the Lord sends thunder and rain. The people are filled with awe of the Lord and of His prophet.

f.w: the LORD sent thunder and rain

n: Terrified, the people beg Samuel to pray for them, admitting that asking for a king added to their sins.
Samuel comforts them: don't be afraid. You have sinned, but don't stop following the Lord now. Keep serving Him with all your heart — repentance looks forward.
Don't turn to worthless idols that cannot help or save you. They are empty.

f.g: Hebrew tohu — emptiness, nothingness; the same word as “without form” in Genesis 1:2.

n: The Lord will not abandon His people, for the sake of His own name and because He chose to make them His. God's covenant faithfulness is the foundation of their hope.

f.w: the LORD will not forsake his people

n: Samuel promises never to stop praying for them; he would consider that a sin. He will keep teaching them the right way. A beautiful model of a faithful leader.

f.w: God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you

n: The heart of Samuel's message: fear the Lord and serve Him sincerely with your whole heart, remembering the great things He has done.

f.w: consider how great things he hath done for you

n: A final warning: if they persist in wickedness, both they and their king will be swept away — fulfilled centuries later in the exile.
